messages.content: I want to develop a stochastic subgrid closure that preserves energy budgets and transfers extreme-precipitation statistics across warming climates. What would make that goal concrete?

There are two explicit requirements. Under held-out 4 K warming, the closure should reduce the absolute 99th-percentile precipitation bias by 20% versus a deterministic closure. It should also keep the global energy-budget residual below 0.5 W/m² without climate-specific retuning. Together, those requirements call for improved extreme-precipitation statistics without giving up the stated energy-budget constraint.
When you say the precipitation bias should fall by 20%, is that a change in the percentile value itself?

No. The comparison concerns the absolute bias of the 99th-percentile precipitation statistic. If the deterministic closure has an absolute bias of B under the held-out 4 K warming condition, a 20% reduction would put the stochastic closure’s absolute bias at 0.8B or less. That does not mean precipitation’s 99th-percentile value must fall by 20%.
Why does the word “absolute” matter there?

It makes the requirement about the magnitude of the bias, rather than its sign. An overestimate and an underestimate can each have an absolute bias. The stated goal is to make that magnitude smaller than the deterministic closure’s by the specified amount; it does not prescribe which side of the reference value the estimate must lie on.
And the deterministic closure is the comparison for that precipitation requirement?

Yes. The 20% improvement is explicitly relative to a deterministic closure. The energy-budget requirement is stated separately as a threshold: the global residual must be below 0.5 W/m² without climate-specific retuning.
What is the significance of the warming case being held out?

It makes the 4 K warming condition a test of transfer rather than merely a condition named in the development goal. The requested precipitation improvement has to appear under that held-out condition. The node does not specify how the held-out case is constructed or how the percentile is estimated, so those details should not be treated as settled.
Does “transfers extreme-precipitation statistics across warming climates” ask for more than the numerical test?

It expresses the broader aim: the closure’s treatment of extreme precipitation should remain useful across warming climates. The explicit numerical precipitation requirement is narrower and more testable: under held-out 4 K warming, reduce absolute 99th-percentile precipitation bias by 20% versus a deterministic closure. The broader phrase should not be mistaken for an additional quantified threshold.
What does the energy condition rule out?

It rules out satisfying the stated goal while leaving a global energy-budget residual of 0.5 W/m² or more. It also rules out relying on climate-specific retuning to keep that residual below the threshold. The requirement does not, by itself, specify a closure architecture or claim that every local energy exchange is individually constrained.
So “below 0.5 W/m²” is strict, not approximately equal to it?

As written, yes: below 0.5 W/m², rather than equal to 0.5 W/m². The unit is watts per square meter, and the stated quantity is the global energy-budget residual. No particular calculation procedure for that residual is supplied here.
Could I describe the stochastic part as simply adding variability to precipitation?

That would be too narrow as a description of the goal. The goal names a stochastic subgrid closure, but it does not specify what is sampled or how stochastic behavior is implemented. Whatever form it takes, it needs to meet both stated requirements: the extreme-precipitation bias comparison under held-out 4 K warming and the global energy-budget residual threshold without climate-specific retuning. Adding variability alone would not establish either outcome.
I also don’t want “preserves energy budgets” to sound like a claim that the closure has already passed a test.

Then it is best phrased as an objective. For example: “Develop a stochastic subgrid closure intended to preserve energy budgets and transfer extreme-precipitation statistics across warming climates, with a global energy-budget residual below 0.5 W/m² without climate-specific retuning and a 20% reduction in absolute 99th-percentile precipitation bias versus a deterministic closure under held-out 4 K warming.” That states the target without presenting it as an achieved result.
Does the energy threshold apply only to precipitation extremes?

No. It is a global energy-budget residual requirement, separate from the precipitation statistic. The two requirements constrain different aspects of the closure: one concerns an extreme-precipitation bias comparison, while the other concerns the global energy budget. Neither can stand in for the other.
Would meeting the precipitation target alone demonstrate the cross-climate objective?

It would meet the specified precipitation test only if the 20% absolute-bias reduction is achieved under held-out 4 K warming relative to the deterministic closure. The goal also requires the global energy-budget residual to stay below 0.5 W/m² without climate-specific retuning. A precipitation improvement on its own would not satisfy the full stated goal.
What should remain unspecified when I discuss this goal?

The supplied goal does not fix the stochastic formulation, training procedure, precipitation reference, percentile-estimation method, or energy-residual calculation. Those may matter in carrying out an evaluation, but naming particular choices now would add details that are not in the stated goal. The firm points are the held-out 4 K warming condition, the 20% reduction in absolute 99th-percentile precipitation bias versus a deterministic closure, and the global residual below 0.5 W/m² without climate-specific retuning.

For the stochastic subgrid closure, I’m considering a CAPE–humidity-conditioned, heavy-tailed stochastic convection closure. The sampled tendencies would be projected onto column energy and water budgets. How does that proposal fit the goal?

It is a proposed way to connect the two parts of the goal. Conditioning on CAPE and humidity makes the stochastic convection closure responsive to those aspects of the column state. A heavy-tailed formulation leaves room for comparatively large sampled outcomes, which is relevant to representing extremes. Projecting the sampled tendencies onto column energy and water budgets addresses the need for budget consistency. None of those design choices, on its own, establishes that the closure will meet the goal’s performance requirements.
What does “CAPE–humidity-conditioned” commit me to saying?

It says the stochastic behavior of the convection closure depends on CAPE and humidity, rather than being specified independently of them. CAPE is convective available potential energy. The proposal does not say how those quantities enter the conditioning, what functional relationship to use, or how strong their influence should be.
Is the heavy tail meant to guarantee better extreme precipitation?

No. “Heavy-tailed” describes a proposed feature of the stochastic closure: relatively large outcomes remain more prominent than they would under a light-tailed formulation. That makes it pertinent to an extreme-precipitation goal, but it is not a guarantee of improved 99th-percentile precipitation bias or of transfer across warming climates. Those remain outcomes to assess, not consequences to assume.
I’m trying to be precise about the order of operations. Is it the random samples that are constrained?

The wording specifies sampled tendencies followed by a projection onto column energy and water budgets. So the budget treatment applies to the tendencies that have been sampled. It does not specify the exact sampling procedure or the mathematical form of the projection.
Why refer to both energy and water budgets at the column level?

Because the proposal explicitly asks the sampled tendencies to respect both column energy and column water budgets. Convection can be discussed in terms of tendencies affecting those budgets, and a projection provides a way to make budget consistency part of the closure design. The proposal does not assign numerical tolerances to the column-level constraints or specify which tendency components the projection changes.
Could I say the projection ensures the global energy-budget target is met?

That would overstate what the proposal establishes. Projecting sampled tendencies onto column budgets is a design choice aimed at budget consistency. Whether the resulting closure meets a global energy-budget requirement is a separate question; a column-level projection should not be presented as proof of a particular global outcome.
And could the projection interfere with the heavy-tailed behavior?

It could affect the sampled tendencies, since projection modifies or constrains them to satisfy the specified budgets. The proposal does not state how much the projection changes their distribution or what effect it has on precipitation extremes. It is therefore useful to keep the two ideas distinct: heavy-tailed sampling is proposed for the stochastic convection behavior, while projection imposes column energy and water budget consistency on the sampled tendencies.
Does the proposal specify a particular heavy-tailed distribution?

No. It calls for a heavy-tailed stochastic convection closure but names no probability distribution, tail parameter, or sampling algorithm. Choosing one would be an implementation detail beyond what is stated here.
Does conditioning on CAPE and humidity imply those are the only possible inputs?

The proposal specifically identifies CAPE and humidity as conditioning variables. It does not explicitly say they are the only inputs, and it does not specify any others. Describing it as CAPE–humidity-conditioned preserves the proposal without turning silence about other inputs into a firm exclusion or an added design choice.
How should I describe the relationship between the stochastic sampling and the budget projection in one sentence?

You could say: “Use a CAPE–humidity-conditioned, heavy-tailed stochastic convection closure, then project its sampled tendencies onto column energy and water budgets.” That keeps the conditioning, tail behavior, sampled tendencies, and budget projection in the proposal without claiming a result.
Would it be fair to describe this as a candidate route to transferring extreme-precipitation statistics across warming climates?

Yes, if “candidate” remains explicit. The heavy-tailed, CAPE–humidity-conditioned formulation is proposed in service of that broader objective, while the column-budget projection addresses budget consistency. The proposal does not report that cross-climate transfer has occurred or establish how well it would perform under warming.
I want to avoid making “stochastic” sound like it means unconstrained noise.

That distinction is central to this proposal. The tendencies are stochastic and conditioned on CAPE and humidity; they are not described as arbitrary, state-independent draws. After sampling, they are projected onto column energy and water budgets. So the proposed randomness sits alongside state dependence and explicit budget constraints, rather than replacing them.
Does “column” here mean I’ve specified a way to close the entire global budget?

No. “Column” identifies the level at which the proposed energy and water budget projection is applied to sampled tendencies. It should not be expanded into a claim that all global budget behavior is thereby determined. The broader budget objective remains something the closure would need to satisfy.
What is the main limitation of what I can claim from this proposal alone?

You can describe the intended design, but not its measured effects. The proposal specifies CAPE–humidity conditioning, heavy-tailed stochastic convection, and projection of sampled tendencies onto column energy and water budgets. It does not provide results for extreme precipitation, establish transfer across warming climates, or demonstrate a global energy-budget outcome.
How can sampled convective extremes reflect CAPE and humidity while satisfying column energy and water conservation?

The two aims can be treated as distinct requirements on the same sampled tendencies. CAPE and humidity condition what the stochastic convection closure samples, including its potential for extreme outcomes. A subsequent projection constrains those sampled tendencies to satisfy the column energy and water budgets. The central question is whether the budget-consistent tendencies still retain the intended dependence on CAPE and humidity and the intended behavior of extremes; the proposal alone does not establish that they do.
Does conservation mean an extreme sample has to be rejected?

Not necessarily. An extreme sample and a budget constraint are not inherently contradictory: a large tendency can be accompanied by other tendencies that balance it within the column. But whether a particular sampled outcome can be accommodated, and how projection would change it, depend on details not specified here. Conservation should not be taken to mean either that all extremes disappear or that every sampled extreme survives unchanged.
What, specifically, is supposed to reflect CAPE and humidity?

In the proposed closure, it is the sampling of convective tendencies that is conditioned on CAPE and humidity. For the question you’ve posed, it also matters whether that state dependence remains apparent after projection. Otherwise, a sample could be conditioned on CAPE and humidity before the budget step but lose the relevant dependence in the budget-consistent output.
So is conditioning something that happens before conservation is imposed?

That is the order implied by the proposal: sample from a CAPE–humidity-conditioned stochastic convection closure, then project the sampled tendencies onto column energy and water budgets. It does not specify the equations for either operation. The useful distinction is between the distribution from which tendencies are sampled and the budget-consistent tendencies produced after projection.
Could I think of the projection as just scaling down a large convective tendency?

That would be only one possible mental picture, not something specified by the proposal. Projection means bringing the sampled tendencies into compliance with the column energy and water budgets; it does not, by itself, say that the operation is a uniform rescaling or that its effect is always to reduce an extreme. Its form matters because different projections could affect the resulting extremes differently.
If the projection changes the draw, in what sense is the result still stochastic?

The result can still vary from one draw to another even though each output is constrained. Stochastic does not require unconstrained outcomes. What matters here is that the final, budget-consistent tendencies retain meaningful variation associated with the CAPE–humidity-conditioned sampling. That retention is a design and evaluation question, not an automatic consequence of calling the closure stochastic.
Is satisfying both budgets a single constraint?

They are two budget requirements: column energy conservation and column water conservation. The proposal says to project sampled tendencies onto both. It does not specify how the requirements are expressed or reconciled within the projection, so it would be premature to describe a particular constraint system.
Why can’t I focus only on conserving energy if extreme precipitation is the statistical target?

Because the question and proposal explicitly include column water conservation as well as column energy conservation. Extreme precipitation is connected to the water budget, while the closure must also respect the energy budget. Treating one as a substitute for the other would leave part of the proposed constraint unaddressed.
Could strong CAPE or high humidity simply force an extreme outcome?

Conditioning does not, by itself, make an extreme outcome compulsory. It means CAPE and humidity inform the stochastic behavior; the proposal does not specify the direction or strength of either relationship for any particular state. Likewise, a heavy-tailed formulation allows for comparatively prominent extremes without saying that every favorable-looking state produces one.
How would I tell whether the conservation step has washed out the state dependence?

Conceptually, you would distinguish the conditioned samples from the final projected tendencies and ask whether the latter still show the intended variation with CAPE and humidity. You would also ask whether the behavior of extremes remains present after projection. That frames what needs to be checked without presuming a particular diagnostic, dataset, or outcome.
What if the sampled tendency already satisfies both column budgets?

In that case, the sample already meets the stated conservation conditions, so there is no budget discrepancy for the projection to correct. Whether a particular projection leaves such a sample exactly unchanged is a property of its definition, which has not been specified. The important point is that budget compliance and stochastic sampling need not be opposing features.
Does preserving the water budget mean precipitation itself has to stay fixed during projection?

No such rule is stated. Column water conservation constrains the balance of water-related tendencies; it does not specify which individual quantity, if any, must remain fixed when a sampled outcome is projected. Since the precipitation extremes are of interest, the effect of projection on them cannot be assumed away.
And conserving energy at the column level would settle the broader energy-budget issue?

Not on its own. Column energy conservation is the constraint placed on sampled tendencies in this proposal. It is relevant to the broader energy-budget objective, but it is not a demonstration of any particular global energy-budget residual. The local design principle and the broader performance requirement should remain distinct.
Can you put the central tension in plain language?

The closure needs room to sample unusually strong convective behavior in ways that depend on CAPE and humidity, but it cannot let those samples create uncompensated column energy or water. Constraining the samples may change them, so the key issue is whether the final conserved outcomes still express the intended extremes and state dependence.
Then what would be an appropriately cautious answer to my original question?

Sample convective tendencies from a heavy-tailed distribution conditioned on CAPE and humidity, and project those tendencies onto the column energy and water budgets. That is the proposed way to combine state-dependent extremes with conservation. Whether the projected outcomes retain the desired extreme-precipitation behavior is an open question rather than a result established by the proposal.

I’d like to make the proposed answer more specific as a hypothesis: CAPE–humidity-conditioned Pareto draws with projection will reduce 4 K P99 bias by at least 20% versus a deterministic closure, while maintaining a global energy-budget residual below 0.5 W/m². Is that a fair statement?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than a reported result. It names a particular heavy-tailed choice—Pareto draws—within the CAPE–humidity-conditioned stochastic convection proposal. It predicts at least a 20% reduction in 4 K P99 precipitation bias relative to the deterministic closure, alongside a global energy-budget residual strictly below 0.5 W/m². Both predicted outcomes still need to be established.
What is more specific here than in the general heavy-tailed proposal?

The hypothesis identifies Pareto draws rather than leaving the heavy-tailed form unspecified. It also makes a quantitative prediction about the 4 K P99 bias and the global energy-budget residual. It does not specify Pareto parameters, the precise conditioning relationship, or the mathematical form of the projection.
Does “at least 20%” include exactly 20%?

Yes. A reduction of at least 20% includes exactly 20% and larger reductions. In the precipitation comparison, the percentage refers to improvement in bias relative to the deterministic closure, not to a 20% decrease in the P99 precipitation value itself.
I mean the magnitude of the P99 bias, not just a change in its sign.

Then “at least a 20% reduction in absolute P99 precipitation bias versus a deterministic closure” makes that meaning explicit. If the deterministic closure’s absolute bias is B for the 4 K comparison, the hypothesized outcome is an absolute bias no greater than 0.8B. That is an interpretation of the threshold, not a claim about a measured bias.
What does choosing Pareto draws contribute to the hypothesis?

A Pareto form is heavy-tailed, so it offers a specific way to hypothesize comparatively prominent extreme draws. Conditioning those draws on CAPE and humidity is intended to connect the stochastic behavior to the convective state. Neither feature guarantees an improvement in P99 precipitation bias: the prediction concerns the outcome after the closure and its projection are taken together.
Should I say CAPE and humidity determine the size of every draw?

That would say more than the hypothesis specifies. “CAPE–humidity-conditioned” means the draws depend on CAPE and humidity in some way; it does not say that those variables uniquely determine each sampled outcome or prescribe how they affect the Pareto form. The draws remain stochastic.
And what role does projection play in this version?

It carries forward the proposed constraint on sampled convective tendencies: after sampling, they are projected onto column energy and water budgets. The hypothesis is that this combination can retain useful extreme-precipitation behavior while maintaining the stated global energy-budget residual. Projection is part of the proposed mechanism, not proof that either quantitative prediction will hold.
Is there a contradiction between Pareto extremes and a column budget constraint?

Not necessarily. A large sampled convective tendency could be compatible with column conservation when the relevant tendencies balance. But projection may change a draw to satisfy the column energy and water budgets. The hypothesis depends on the final, projected behavior—not merely on the existence of large unprojected Pareto draws.
So I shouldn’t assume the projected outcomes still follow a Pareto distribution exactly?

Correct. The hypothesis specifies Pareto draws with projection; it does not assert that the projected tendencies retain an exact Pareto distribution. The projection’s effect on the tail is part of why the predicted P99 bias reduction remains a hypothesis.
How should I distinguish the column constraints from the energy number?

The projection concerns column energy and water budgets for sampled tendencies. The numerical prediction concerns a global energy-budget residual below 0.5 W/m². They are related in the proposed approach, but they are not the same statement: imposing column constraints does not, by itself, demonstrate the global threshold.
Does the hypothesis say how close to zero the global residual will be?

No. It predicts only that the global energy-budget residual will be below 0.5 W/m². It does not assign a particular value beneath that threshold, and an outcome equal to 0.5 W/m² would not satisfy the strict “below” wording.
Could the precipitation part succeed even if the energy part fails?

They are distinct predicted outcomes, so one could be observed without the other. The hypothesis as stated predicts both: at least a 20% reduction in the 4 K P99 bias relative to the deterministic closure and a global energy-budget residual below 0.5 W/m². Meeting only one would not establish the full hypothesis.
Does this answer the question about reflecting CAPE and humidity while conserving energy and water?

It offers a specific hypothesized answer: condition Pareto draws on CAPE and humidity, then project the sampled tendencies onto column energy and water budgets. It goes further by predicting quantitative precipitation and global-energy outcomes. It does not yet show that the projected convective extremes retain the intended CAPE–humidity dependence or that the numerical predictions are achieved.
Can you give me one concise wording that keeps its status clear?

“We hypothesize that CAPE–humidity-conditioned Pareto draws, with sampled tendencies projected onto column energy and water budgets, will reduce absolute 4 K P99 precipitation bias by at least 20% versus a deterministic closure while keeping the global energy-budget residual below 0.5 W/m².”
How would you turn the Pareto-draw hypothesis into a plan without treating it as a result?

Fit the Pareto parameters on 0 K and 2 K data, project the sampled tendencies, then compare the held-out 4 K P99 precipitation result against the deterministic closure and audit the energy residual. That is a sequence of planned steps. It does not say that the P99 comparison or the energy audit has already succeeded.
Why name 0 K and 2 K separately from 4 K?

They have different roles in the plan. The 0 K and 2 K data are used to fit the Pareto parameters. The 4 K condition is held out for the P99 comparison, rather than included in that fitting step. Keeping those roles distinct is what makes the 4 K comparison a test of how the fitted closure behaves under the held-out warming condition.
Does the plan call for refitting the Pareto parameters at 4 K?
No. It says to fit them on 0 K and 2 K data and compare at held-out 4 K. Refitting on 4 K data would change the role of the held-out condition described in this plan.
When does the projection happen?

The stated order is to fit the Pareto parameters, project the sampled tendencies, and evaluate the resulting behavior at held-out 4 K. In the proposed closure, the projection is the budget-consistency step applied to sampled tendencies. The plan does not specify its mathematical form.
Should the P99 comparison use the draws before projection or the tendencies after projection?

The comparison should speak to the proposed closure as it is described in the plan, including projection. Comparing only unprojected draws would not tell you how the budget-constrained tendencies perform. The plan does not specify every detail of how precipitation P99 is calculated, but it does make projection part of what is to be evaluated.
What exactly is the deterministic closure doing in this plan?

It is the comparison baseline for the held-out 4 K P99 result. The plan calls for comparing the proposed stochastic closure against that deterministic closure; it does not describe changing the deterministic closure or give a measured outcome for either one.
Is the P99 comparison enough on its own?

No. The plan also calls for an energy-residual audit. The precipitation comparison and the energy audit address different parts of the goal: behavior of an extreme-precipitation statistic at held-out 4 K, and energy-budget behavior. A favorable P99 comparison would not, by itself, establish the energy-budget outcome.
Does projecting onto column budgets make the energy audit redundant?

No. Projecting sampled tendencies onto column energy and water budgets is a step in the proposed method. Auditing the energy residual checks an outcome of the resulting closure. The plan includes both rather than assuming that the projection alone settles the energy-residual question.
What does this plan actually test about transfer across warming climates?

It tests whether Pareto parameters fitted using 0 K and 2 K data yield the intended P99 behavior when evaluated at held-out 4 K, after the sampled tendencies have been projected. That is the transfer question expressed by this particular plan. The plan does not assert that transfer will occur.
Can I say the 0 K and 2 K data prove the Pareto form is right before the 4 K comparison?

No. Fitting Pareto parameters on those data is an action in the plan, not proof that the form is right or that it will work at held-out 4 K. The later P99 comparison is important precisely because fitting and successful held-out behavior are different things.
Does the plan say how CAPE and humidity enter the fitted parameters?

No. The proposed closure is CAPE–humidity-conditioned, but this plan does not specify the conditioning relationship or the fitting procedure. It says which warming conditions supply data for fitting the Pareto parameters, then calls for projection and held-out evaluation.
Would the energy audit be a substitute for checking the water budget?

Not as a description of the proposal. The tendencies are to be projected onto column energy and water budgets, while this plan specifically calls for auditing the energy residual. An energy-residual audit should not be described as though it independently reports a water-budget result; no separate water-budget audit is stated here.
How do I keep the plan from sounding like the hypothesis has already been confirmed?

Use prospective wording: “Fit Pareto parameters on 0 K and 2 K data, project the sampled tendencies, compare held-out 4 K P99 precipitation against the deterministic closure, and audit the energy residual.” Words such as “fit,” “compare,” and “audit” state what will be done. They do not assign a result to the comparison or audit.
What would be an overstatement when describing the held-out comparison?

Saying that the 4 K P99 bias has already improved, or that the energy residual has already passed its requirement, would be an overstatement. The plan identifies the comparisons needed to find out; it supplies no measured P99 bias or audited residual.
Can you restate the sequence once more, keeping the training and evaluation conditions unmistakable?

Use 0 K and 2 K data to fit the Pareto parameters. Project the sampled tendencies onto the proposed column budgets. Then evaluate P99 precipitation at held-out 4 K against the deterministic closure and audit the energy residual. The 4 K condition is for that held-out comparison, not for fitting the Pareto parameters.

For the evaluation, run ten-member held-out 4 K ensembles with frozen parameters. Compare the projected Pareto closure and the deterministic closure on P99 precipitation bias and global energy-budget residual. How should I describe that activity?

Describe it as an evaluation to be run, not as a result: run ten-member ensembles at held-out 4 K without changing the parameters, then compare the projected Pareto and deterministic closures on both P99 precipitation bias and global energy-budget residual. The comparison will test the hypothesis; the activity description does not say which closure performs better.
What does “frozen parameters” establish in this comparison?

It means the parameters are held fixed during the held-out 4 K evaluation. In the stated plan, the Pareto parameters are fitted on 0 K and 2 K data; they are not refitted for the 4 K ensembles. That keeps the held-out condition distinct from the fitting conditions.
Does ten-member mean I can already report how variable the P99 bias is?

No. Ten members specify the ensemble size for the activity, not its observed spread or any resulting bias. The activity calls for running the ensembles and making the comparison; it provides no member-level or aggregate outcomes.
Which version of the stochastic closure belongs in the comparison?

The projected Pareto closure. The sampled tendencies are projected onto column energy and water budgets as part of the proposed closure, so the comparison is about that budget-constrained version, not just the unprojected Pareto draws.
And do I compare the energy residual for both closures, or only for the projected one?

The activity says to compare the projected Pareto and deterministic closures on P99 bias and global energy-budget residual. Both metrics therefore belong in the comparison. It does not provide a measured residual for either closure.
What does the P99 part actually compare?

It compares the closures’ bias in the 99th-percentile precipitation statistic under held-out 4 K warming. For the hypothesized improvement, the relevant comparison is the magnitude of that bias relative to the deterministic closure—not whether the P99 precipitation value itself is 20% smaller.
Can I say that this run will demonstrate a reduction of at least 20%?

You can say it will test that prediction. The hypothesis predicts at least a 20% reduction in absolute 4 K P99 precipitation bias versus the deterministic closure, but the ten-member activity has no reported outcome yet. “Will demonstrate” would presume the comparison’s result.
How does the global energy-budget residual enter that test?

It is the other outcome to compare and audit under held-out 4 K. The hypothesis predicts a global energy-budget residual below 0.5 W/m² for the projected Pareto closure. Running a closure whose tendencies have been projected onto column budgets does not, by itself, report or establish that global residual.
If the P99 comparison looks favorable, could I leave the residual out of the account?

Not if you are describing this activity or assessing the full hypothesis. The activity explicitly compares both P99 bias and global energy-budget residual. A favorable precipitation comparison alone would not answer the energy-budget part.
Does this activity specify how to combine results across the ten members?

No. It specifies ten-member held-out 4 K ensembles and the quantities to compare, but not an aggregation rule, uncertainty calculation, or method for estimating P99 from the ensemble. Those details should not be presented as choices already made here.
Would it be accurate to call the 4 K ensembles a retuning exercise?

No. The parameters are frozen for the held-out 4 K ensembles. The purpose stated here is to compare the projected Pareto and deterministic closures on P99 bias and global energy-budget residual under that condition, not to adjust parameters to it.
Does “ten-member” tell us that the two closures have matched or paired realizations?

No pairing procedure is specified. The activity calls for ten-member held-out 4 K ensembles and a comparison between closures, but it does not say how individual members correspond or whether any randomness is shared.
What is the clearest one-sentence description that keeps the whole activity prospective?
“Run ten-member ensembles at held-out 4 K with parameters frozen, and compare the projected Pareto closure with the deterministic closure on P99 precipitation bias and global energy-budget residual.”
What did the held-out 4 K comparison show for P99 precipitation bias and the energy residual?

The projected closure’s absolute P99 precipitation bias was 7.8 mm/day, compared with 10.5 mm/day for the deterministic closure. That is a reported 26% reduction in absolute bias. The reported global energy-budget residual was 0.31 W/m².
Can you show how the 26% figure follows from those bias values?
The absolute-bias difference is 10.5 − 7.8 = 2.7 mm/day. Dividing that difference by the deterministic closure’s 10.5 mm/day bias gives about 0.257, or 25.7%, which rounds to 26%.
Is the 2.7 mm/day difference a change in the P99 precipitation amount?

No. It is the difference between two *absolute P99 biases*: 10.5 and 7.8 mm/day. The reported figures do not give the P99 precipitation amounts themselves or indicate whether either closure overestimated or underestimated them.
What can I say about the energy number without reading too much into it?

You can report that the global energy-budget residual in the held-out 4 K result was 0.31 W/m². That is a global residual, not a numerical report of each column’s energy or water budget. No deterministic-closure energy residual is supplied in this result, so it does not establish an energy-residual comparison between the two closures.
Does the result tell us what happened to individual extreme draws after projection?

No. It reports the resulting absolute P99 bias, its comparison with the deterministic closure, and the global energy-budget residual. It does not show individual draws, how projection changed them, or the distribution of outcomes across ensemble members.
Would it be accurate to call the 26% reduction a reduction in error magnitude?

Yes, provided you identify the error precisely: it is a 26% reduction in the magnitude of the P99 precipitation bias relative to the deterministic closure under held-out 4 K warming. It is not a statement that all precipitation errors fell by 26%.
How narrowly should I frame the evidence?

Frame it as the reported held-out 4 K result. The numbers describe absolute P99 precipitation bias for the projected and deterministic closures under that condition, plus a global energy-budget residual of 0.31 W/m². They do not, by themselves, quantify behavior at other warming levels or establish how the closure behaves for every precipitation statistic.
Give me a compact results sentence with the units and comparison intact.

“Under held-out 4 K warming, the projected closure had an absolute P99 precipitation bias of 7.8 mm/day versus 10.5 mm/day for the deterministic closure—a 26% reduction—and the reported global energy-budget residual was 0.31 W/m².”

I want to examine the two design choices separately. Ablate CAPE–humidity conditioning and budget projection in frozen-parameter 4 K ensembles, then assess P99 precipitation bias and the energy residual. How should I frame that activity?

Frame it as two separate ablations under the 4 K condition. In one, remove CAPE–humidity conditioning while retaining budget projection. In the other, remove budget projection while retaining CAPE–humidity conditioning. Keep parameters frozen for the ensembles and assess P99 precipitation bias and the energy residual for each variant. The activity sets up comparisons; it does not state their outcomes.
When I say “separately,” am I also asking for a run with both features removed?

Not as stated. “Ablate CAPE–humidity conditioning and budget projection separately” calls for isolating each removal rather than treating a combined removal as the test of either feature. A variant with both removed is not specified in this activity.
What would the conditioning ablation tell me?

It is intended to probe the contribution of CAPE–humidity conditioning to the behavior of the closure in the frozen-parameter 4 K ensembles, while budget projection remains in place. P99 bias and energy residual are the stated quantities to assess. The activity does not predict whether either quantity will improve, worsen, or remain similar.
And what does the projection ablation isolate?

It probes the role of budget projection while retaining CAPE–humidity conditioning.
